*1) Term foreigner*
So under LT law, “foreigner” is considered someone without the LT citizenship (LR įstatymo dėl užsieniečių teisinės padėties 2 str. 32 p. - *Užsienietis* – asmuo, kuris nėra Lietuvos Respublikos pilietis, neatsižvelgiant į tai, ar jis turi kurios nors užsienio valstybės pilietybę, ar neturi jokios.).



*2) Regarding the risk of compensation*

To reduce the risk of reclassification while still achieving our goal:

# *Structure it as a voluntary benefit/discount*
#* Emphasise that drivers are free to choose whether to participate.
#* Ideally, give them a choice of providers (if there are a few), or frame it as Bolt having negotiated “discounts” with schools.
# *Cost-sharing*
#* Require some co-payment (even symbolic, like 10% as you mentioned) to signal independent investment.
# *Frame it as a partnership, not employment training*
#* Position it as “community support” or “preferred partner pricing” rather than mandatory onboarding or training. Maybe we can sign partnership agreement (with some school) like with Bolt Rewards Program where we fund and give 90% discount to the drivers and they only need to pay 10% that’s left (or something similar).
#* Avoid language that implies performance conditions (“to improve your work for Bolt”) - instead use wording like “to help you integrate into Lithuania more easily.” or similar.
# *Avoid performance linkage*
#* Don’t tie course participation to ratings, bonuses, access to orders, or platform benefits. That would be a huge employment red flag.
# *Tax treatment clarity*
#* [~accountid:62ea2a695111209f4fde8265] could you please advise us whether this counts as non-taxable education support or taxable benefit in kind and suggest structure accordingly to avoid retroactive liabilities.

So to minimise the reclass risk as much as possible, my suggestion in this situation would be to create such structure where Bolt pays partial coverage (for example, Bolt negotiating a bulk discount with language schools) to schools, drivers pay 10%. The cost-sharing reinforces the idea that drivers are *independent professionals investing in their own upskilling*, thus in some way mitigating *employer-style investment in staff training* idea.

* _No drivers accepted the trip and, as a result, the app returned status messages to Mr. Borg that “no driver available” (or equivalent) rather than a driver cancellation after acceptance._
* _Because no driver accepted the booking, the ride could not proceed, and no contract of carriage was conclusively formed between the passenger and a driver (see 4.1–4.2 of our passenger T&Cs)._

*_Contractual & Terms‑based Position_*

_Bolt’s Passenger Terms and Conditions, which every user agrees to when registering on the platform, set out the following key principles:_

* *_Clause 1.1–1.2_* _– The Bolt app is a technology platform that connects passengers with independent drivers. Bolt does not itself provide transport services, nor does it guarantee the availability of such services. The transport contract is concluded directly between passenger and driver, not with Bolt._
* *_Clause 4.1–4.2_* _– A booking becomes binding only when a driver accepts the request. Until then, the passenger’s booking is merely a request broadcast to nearby drivers and not a confirmed service. Where no driver accepts, no transport contract is formed._
* *_Clause 6.1_* _– Bolt expressly disclaims liability in cases where no driver is available or accepts a booking, and the platform does not guarantee uninterrupted or error-free service at all times._

_In this case, because no driver accepted the booking:_

# _No transport contract was formed between Mr. Borg and a driver._
# _Bolt has no contractual liability beyond facilitating the request process._
# _The T&Cs expressly exclude liability for consequential or indirect costs (such as alternative transport, parking expenses, or missed flights) arising from lack of driver availability._

_In light of the above, while we regret the inconvenience Mr. Borg experienced, Bolt has fulfilled its contractual obligations under the Passenger Terms and Conditions. As no service was provided and no payment was taken, we respectfully submit that there is no basis for compensation of parking fees or related consequential costs._

_We trust this clarifies our position. Please do not hesitate to contact us should you require any further information._

_Yours sincerely,_

hi [~accountid:712020:d008dcec-6cfe-47e4-83a0-c29522744742] ,

I was digging into the “single commission invoice row” setting in the admin panel and wanted to sanity check what’s right for France from both a compliance and reclassification perspective.

Looking at the itemized invoice (like FR1125-201120)::

* *Legally*, under *Article L441-9 of the French Commercial Code* and *Article 242 nonies A of the CGI*, invoices issued B2B must clearly state the *nature of services, unit prices, quantities, VAT treatment*, etc. If we only show a lump-sum “platform fee,” it risks not meeting those standards.
* Our *T&Cs for VTC (Art. 4.17)* and *Taxi (Art. 4.18)* explicitly say that Bolt will issue *detailed separate invoices* for amounts owed by fleets. So a single-line invoice isn’t really aligned with that.
* *From a reclassification risk angle*, the itemized format is better: it gives transparency into how commissions are calculated, shows the fleet has visibility over their earnings and deductions, and helps demonstrate independence (vs. Bolt just “paying” them a flat amount, which is more employer-like).

Do you agree we should treat the itemized format as the standard in France and clean up any cases where “single row” is still on?

Curious if you see it differently! Maybe also better to bouble check with Tax their view, WFYT?

thanks,

Eli

Hi [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba], I hope that you are well ! 

Please allow us to reach out to you regarding the invoices sent to drivers in France.

The issue is detailed in the description, but essentially: the invoices are not standardised - some are issued with a detailed invoice, and others only have a single amount. 

Looking at the itemized invoice (like FR1125-201120):

* *Legally*, under *Article L441-9 of the French Commercial Code* and *Article 242 nonies A of the CGI*, invoices issued B2B must clearly state the *nature of services, unit prices, quantities, VAT treatment*, etc. If we only show a lump-sum “platform fee,” it risks not meeting those standards.
* Our *T&Cs for PHVs (Art. 4.17)* and *Taxi (Art. 4.18)* explicitly say that Bolt will issue *detailed separate invoices* for amounts owed by fleets. So a single-line invoice isn’t really aligned with that.
* *From a reclassification risk angle*, the itemized format is better: it gives transparency into how commissions are calculated, shows the fleet has visibility over their earnings and deductions, and helps demonstrate independence (vs. Bolt just “paying” them a flat amount, which is more employer-like). 



Kindly could you share your thoughts on this and confirm if we can standardise all invoices to include an itemised invoice?



Thank you !

*Methodology*

* Considered each user’s *last* {{order_try}} during the observation window (June–August).
* Categorized the outcome of that {{order_try}} as:
** *Success* – order was finished.
** *Failure: driver-related* – rejected by driver or no response.
** *Failure: other reasons* – e.g. rider cancellation, payment issue, or driver cancellation after accepting.
* Tracked user activity for *30 days after the last order_try*. Each user had a 30-day observation window.
* Calculated the share of users who completed at least one order within this 30-day period.

*Results*

* Users with finished orders show a significantly higher return rate compared to those without (*–11.2pp to –17.3pp difference*).
* The most notable finding is for *driver rejection*: return rate drops *–17.3pp vs. Cohort A* and *–6.1pp vs. Cohort C*.

Hi [~accountid:712020:9cfda827-f644-48a1-9da8-aff3fd427bf9] !

Thank you for sharing this initiative in the context of the Guimarães re-launch. 

We would like to provide some legal context and considerations before your team decides how to move forward:

As far as I know, all initiatives related to Bolt-branded courier bags have been “discontinued” and the bags are currently sold through a third-party service provider with no direct connection to Bolt. Relaunching a campaign of this nature – where Bolt itself distributes branded bags – involves certain risks that should not be underestimated.

By way of background, when reclassification inspections were intensified by the labour authority (ACT), they would stop couriers on the street and would interrogate them. One of the main reasons why we currently face relatively few reclassification claims is that, at the time, very few couriers used Bolt-branded backpacks. 

On other hand, the use of branded equipment (such as a Bolt backpack) is a recurring element that courts rely on to support the existence of an employment relationship. The fact that Bolt does not require or impose the use of branded bags has been an important argument in our favour and has contributed to positive outcomes in litigation.

With this in mind, it is important to acknowledge that couriers who receive Bolt-branded bags through this initiative could, at a later stage, use that fact as evidence against the company in reclassification proceedings.

Following this context, we must conclude that ultimately this is a business decision. 
However, should you wish to proceed, we recommend applying the following mitigation measures:

* Restrict the initiative strictly to Guimarães;
* Limit the distribution to no more than 50 bags;
* Ensure that any communication is channeled exclusively through fleets, with a simple and neutral message (e.g., “Bolt will distribute free bags on [day] at [place]”), avoiding direct engagement with couriers and avoiding any wording that suggests obligation or requirement.
* Do not request couriers to hand in their existing bags – allow them to retain both.

Please feel free to reach out if further clarification is required.

Thank you!!

*New Letter from AKI*

* Follow-up letter received from AKI ([link|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1ChOUHxOa9BXKVmeP-O0papTJBL7peniw]).
** AKI notes that even though we process full suite of data that was provided at Annex 2, in June we only provided a high-level overview of the driver’s complaint to the rider. As such, AKI concludes that the rider has not been provided with all of their data. 
*** In particular, we have failed to provide “Correspondence related to the case and held with the Data Subject”, “Internal notes and conclusions on the case” and”Details of the trip between the driver and the data subject”.
*** AKI asks why we cannot just provide this information in a redacted format.
** AKI notes that we are continuing to store data relating to the incident on the rider’s profile, but there is no indication of purpose or storage duration (particularly given that the allegations were wrong).
** AKI asks the following:
*** _1. Why is it not possible to provide the complainant with information ("Correspondence related to the case and held with the data subject"; "Internal notes and conclusions regarding the case" and "Details of the trip between the manager and the data subject") in a non-personalized form, i.e.,_
_by removing the personal data of the relevant third parties from the information? What, in Bolt's opinion, constitutes an infringement of the rights of third parties if their personal data is removed from the information?_
**** _1.1. If Bolt finds that the information can still be presented to the data subject in an edited form, the AKI requests that the relevant information be disclosed to the complainant and that a copy of the response be submitted to the AKI._
*** _2. How long, for what purpose, and on what legal basis does Bolt plan to retain the data related to the case under the complainant's profile? How is this justified if the complainant was not involved in the case at all? Has the complainant been provided with the relevant information regarding the retention of data?_
* Deadline for our response is {color:#ff5630}*13 October 2025*{color}.

*Thoughts*

* (1)
** AKI has not seen our follow-up response to the rider - this may have been lost in translation. We can provide this, and explain the position. We can also flag to AKI that we explained in our previous response that we would be doing this.
** By confirming we have provided it, we can avoid having to respond to the second point.
** We can also flag that the rider seems satisfied with our response.
* (2)
** We can leverage general retention language, and refer AKI to the privacy notice. In particular:
*** Purposes:
**** To provide CS support services / process feedback
**** To defend Bolt against potential legal claims
*** Legal basis:
**** Legitimate interest
**** (Doubtful that contractual necessity could be used as a legal basis for long-term retention)
*** Duration:
**** Seems likely that this will be 3 years, but check this with ODPO / Tat.
** Still justified even though the rider was not involved, as both of the purposes still apply. We have also updated the rider’s profile for good measure.
** We have directed the complainant to our privacy notice. If AKI continues to push on this point, we can consider sharing more details.

Hey! Apologies for the long wait, as we didn’t have a general rule for such cases set in Poland. The answer would be as follows:

As per the general rule, annual leave in Poland is always calculated in *hours.* If your employment percentage changes during the year, leave must be recalculated proportionally for each period (your case):

* full-time (until March 10),
* part-time (from March 11 onwards).

Your accumulated days will then be:

* *6 days carried over* from 2024 → these remain valid and are not reduced, since they are already earned rights.
* *5 days accrued in 2025 up to March 10 (full-time)* → these need to be recalculated because your daily schedule has changed.

Conversion after switching to 75% (6h/day)

* Your *11 days total (6 + 5)* are currently counted as:
*  11 × 8h = *88 hours* of leave.
* After switching to 75%, your workday is *6 hours*. So:
*  88 ÷ 6h = *14.67 days → rounded up = 15 days* of leave (at 6 hours per day).

Therefore, the takeaway is as follows:

* You don’t lose any leave — it’s simply *recalculated into hours* and then converted into “days” based on your new daily hours.
* Your 11 days before March become effectively *15 leave days of 6 hours each*.
* Any new leave accrued from March 11 onward will be calculated according to your 75% FTE (so 20 days annually instead of 26).



Hopefully that answers your question!

According to the[ Estonian Tax Information Act|https://www.riigiteataja.ee/en/eli/ee/Riigikogu/act/521052024003/consolide]:  

h3. *§ 20*^*22*^*.*  Seller

 (1) For the purposes of this Act, a seller is a person or legal arrangement that is registered on the platform and is engaged in activities covered by a reporting obligation or to whom a fee is paid or credited relating to this activity.

 (2) A seller covered by reporting is a seller who is a resident of a Member State or a seller that leases or rents out immovable property or a part thereof located in a Member State. *_Also, the seller covered by reporting is a seller who is a resident of a third country or jurisdiction listed on the webpage of the Tax and Customs Board_*, or a seller who leases or rents out immovable property or a part thereof located in such a country or jurisdiction.

In short it’s: Discount × (1 – Cost-sharing %) ÷ (1 + Assumed VAT) → 10.31 × (1-40%) ÷ (1+20%) = 5.16

And commission from total discount amount: Discount × (1 – cost-sharing %) × contractual commission % → 10.31 × (1-40%) × 28% = 1.7338

Hope this helps!

* *Is this a part of the global Bolt Kiosk initiative?*
Yes, it is part of the global Bolt Kiosk initiative. Currently in the testing phase to tailor it specifically for our market. 
* *Which country does this apply to?*
Tanzania.
* *What data exactly will riders share with the agent?*
Riders will share their *phone number* with the agent, the pick up and drop off location. Once the ride is booked, they will receive an SMS containing their ride details — including the vehicle plate number, driver’s phone number (for contact) and a link to track or share their ride.
* *From which agencies will that agent be from? My understanding is that they will not be Bolt’s agents - am I correct?*
Correct. They will not be Bolt employees. The agents will be third-party businesses (e.g. shops, kiosks and potentially venues such as malls or transport terminals) who will be facilitating the ride bookings.

We plan to present this initiative to drivers as an onboarding bonus campaign, targeted at new registrations who join through the gas station event.
# *Event Duration & Scope*
The campaign will likely run over 2–3 days, depending on driver attendance, until all 200 cards have been distributed. Once completed, we will evaluate results internally and decide whether it makes sense to repeat the initiative in Athens to further boost supply.
# *Driver Eligibility*
Drivers must have fully submitted all documents required for activation before receiving a card. If any document is missing at the event, the card will be given only once the driver completes their file.
# *Card Distribution*
Coral will deliver the prepaid cards to our Athens office after payment. The local Ops team together with OS agents will then manage the gas station event, coordinating registrations and distributing cards. Fully activated drivers will receive their card on the spot; those pending documents will get theirs later, either at the driver center or at the next event.

* Stability and job security
* Long-term career growth
* A company with a clear future and strong foundation

This article would aim to highlight Bolt as a stable, future-focused employer, while showing that engineers here work on cutting-edge, meaningful projects with real impact – a combination rarely found in the local market.

*Format:* Interview-based storytelling, with integrated quotes from all three engineers

*SLAs*
I won’t go to details with the SLAs since you have done it already and I added one good example in the comment [HERE|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1CZIBRTP0plLqrmjfep4pwJnOnb4TvLzDlU8gj2vWsGI/edit?disco=AAABsrkVXzI]. *But one example what may happen with SLAs if we agree with the Dispatch and Delivery SLAs they have proposed:*
A) Bolt sends Order to Kinara on Monday after 12pm. In such case Kinara may send the info to its warehouse partner for dispatch next working day - Tuesday
B) On Tuesday Kinara sends order for dispatch to its warehouse partner also for some reason after 12pm
C) Warehouse partner may dispatch such order Thursday
D) And then on top of it there will be delivery times 1-2 days or 3-5 days from Thursday. If weekend comes between then this prolongs the delivery even more bc they have said that delivery times excludes non-working days.
E) So in worse case scenario if Order was made to Kinara on Monday after 12pm then equipment would be delivered next week’s Friday. Total time from Bolt’s order on Monday to delivery would be then (counting from Monday, i.e. “0 day”) 12 days
This case is even worser if we should submit order to Kinara on Friday after 12pm.

Before the above is not aligned under clauses (3.3.b and 3.5.a) there is not point to review the SLA calculation tables since those tables should reflect the above.

*PS!* Ofc it might be that those worse case scenarios won’t happen and in reality they deliver things quickly. However, you have to be aware of the above use cases and the rights they want to leave for themselves.

*Insurance:* Ekta had to come back with this, but not sure where this stands [@aleksandr.parshikov|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U036FKK4E15] ?Kinara has proposed sth which our insurance team should review.

*IP clause:* IP team should review it since they proposed totally new chapter

*Liability:* ok to exclude some (not all) third party, etc losses. Ok to exclude indirect losses for both sides. Needs more through look and is also dependant on
a) how the insurance goes
b) what is the total term (i.e. 5 months vs 3 months trial + extension to 1 year).
If they are obliged to have some insurance then we can be more collaborative here since we know that if sth happens with tablets insurance covers the costs and we don’t have a gap in monetary side as well as in the supply chain.

*SLA breach & penalties*: depending what is the total term, etc we might be a bit flexible, but not in a way they have proposed. For pilot time not having penalties unless difference in SLA targets is significant (e.g. 70%) - might be ok + show our goodwill (similar approach as with Cognizant, basically giving small grace period). 

However, if after pilot period agreement should be extended then penalties should kick in and having 8% there seems too low. The penalties we proposed initially in table form are reasonable especially considering that they are implemented only for the market that lack not for all markets.

*Returning items in case of termination/expiry:* they didn’t agree with our proposal which was reasonable *-* Bolt bears the return related costs if termination is initiated by Bolt under cls 3.2 or contract expires. For all other cases, Kinara should cover the costs since in such cases termination would be done due to the breach of obligations by Kinara. We shouldn’t pay return costs of Equipment in case Kinara has breached the agreement. We already have a loss of reorganising our business, etc. If we also have to bear delivery costs in such case then seems unbalanced. 

However, in the end business decision and not a big blocker  in case of short term pilot with low volumes. Riskier and bigger blocker if we decide to have long-term and E2E relation.

*GENERAL NOTE:*  Ofc we can be here more collaborative and see how in reality they do during the pilot. Especially if pilot term is short and volumes low. They might not want to invest and risk that much since they haven’t had any collaboration with us before.
However, we also have to think what tone it sets for E2E solution from our side and how it reflects their approach for E2E. If for the pilot there are lot of red flags, then those will be carried over more or less to E2E project. Also, we are already sharing the same terms which we want to see in E2E solution. And there we are way more open to risks and effect on our business is greater.

* Bolt currently has a partnership with Autodoc, which offers drivers discounts on spare parts on Autodoc’s website (i.e., part of Bolt Rewards Program).

*** Between Bolt Ops Ou and German Autodoc entity.
*** Discounts are provided to drivers in France, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Poland.
*** Appears to be a classic Bolt Rewards contract - Bolt makes Autodoc’s offer available to drivers (i.e., marketing), Autodoc provides the drivers with discounts. Bolt can use metrics to improve the program.
*** Parties are independent controllers. Each party shall indemnify the other. DSA must be implemented to the extent the parties share any personal data (none has been entered, on the basis that Felix Antwi claimed “_No personal data will be shared_”).
* Bolt now wants to launch the Autodoc offer “in new markets that were not covered in the initial agreement”. As such an updated Addendum has been prepared (earliest attachment - *Addendum 1*).
** Apparently, we will be asking the partner to share redemption data and so a second addendum has also been prepared (second attachment - *Addendum 2*) (however, the ticket description says “_No personal data will be shared_”).
* *Request*: Review the Addendum and confirm if any red flags.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Addendum 1: No specific comments ✅ 
** Partner undertakes to now also provide the discounts in the following countries: *Denmark*, *Netherlands*, *Latvia*, *Greece*, *Austria*, *Estonia*, *Czech* *Republic*, *Finland*, *Slovakia*, *Portugal*, *Hungary*, *Lithuania*, *Norway*, *Romania*, *Switzerland*, and *Italy*.
* Addendum 2: Some minor comments ⚠️ 
** Partner shall provide Bolt with the following data: *Number of drivers that claimed the offer*, *total offer claims*, *total value of transactions* (including discount), and *total value of discounts*.
*** I would add is that we should make it clear that this is AGGREGATED data (i.e., _Change to “5.1. is added as follows: The Partner shall therefore provide Bolt with the following aggregated data:…_”).
*** The inclusion of Clause 2 (“_5.2. is added as follows: Bolt_”) makes no sense.
* General:
** Clause 11.3 of the May agreement requires the parties to enter into a DSA where one shares personal data with the other (regardless of the direction). If the data being shared here is *_personal_* data, then we will have to enter a DSA, regardless of the fact that Bolt appears to be the importer only.
*** However, since these are total numbers, it sounds like the data might be aggregated.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Is this data aggregated data, or relating to specific drivers?
** Is Bolt sending any personal data to Autodoc?
* Advice:
** If the data is aggregated / no personal data is being shared, then I have not comments.
** If the data is not aggregated, we will need to enter into a DSA. However, we need to make sure that it is Bolt-friendly (given that Bolt is the importer).

Hi [~accountid:712020:714baa0e-ddd0-4776-8064-c5a5d3ae37aa] , I’ve now reviewed the music licence proposal. Overall, I {color:#36b37e}*don’t see any high-risk issues*{color}, and I think it’s fine for Bolt to go ahead if you're happy. :green-check: That said, there are a few points worth being aware of before final approval - these aren’t blockers, but they do come with {color:#ff5630}*some light responsibilities for Bolt and things to keep in mind*{color}. I have set these out below…

h2. :red_arrow:  *Obligations / Potential Issues to Consider in the Music Licence Proposal*

h6. 

# +*The licence renews automatically each year (Clauses 3, 9)*+

* *Risk:* Unless we give *1 month’s notice*, the licence will roll over automatically at the end of each year..
* *What this means for Bolt:* We’d need someone to keep an eye on renewal dates to avoid being tied in when music is no longer being used at certain hubs. However, this is low risk as it’s easy to opt out - we just need to manage the renewal dates proactively.

h6. 

# +*Tariff / Pricing Changes Without Cap (Clause 6)*+

* *Risk:* The cost is linked to PPL/PRS’s published tariffs, which they can adjust at any time. These changes do not require Bolt’s consent.
* *What this means for Bolt:* There is no pricing certainty or cap. We could try to negotiate a fixed or capped cost, however the current cost is less than £500/year, so it’s unlikely that future increases will be significant - {color:#ff5630}*please confirm if the business is comfortable accepting this risk*{color}.

h6. 

# +*Strict Data Submission Obligations (Clause 5)*+

* *Risk:* Bolt must submit "Use Details" on request. This appears to include details such as the music source, the duration of playing the music (including days, hours and minutes) and the total number of employees that can hear the music. Bolt may face charges if we provide inaccurate details.
* *What this means for Bolt:* This is more of an FYI of an obligation rather than an issue - we must simply ensure that we can track and retain this data per location.

h6. 

# +*PPL PRS can request to visit sites (Clause 7)*+

* *Risk:* PPL PRS (or their reps) have rights of entry and inspection, including access to accounting records where tariffs are based on revenue or staff numbers.
* *What this means for Bolt:* We should ensure that the hubs are informed of this possibility and are prepared for possible site visits.

h6. 

# +*No Limitation of Liability / Dispute Framework*+

* *Risk:* There is {color:#ff5630}*no limitation of liability for Bolt*{color}, and no built-in dispute resolution process outside litigation.
* *What this means for Bolt:* Bolt may be liable to an uncapped amount and, in the event of overcharging or breach, Bolt’s options are limited. However, given the low fee here, it’s probably not a concern, but we could look to negotiate if we scale this licence up in future. Alternatively, {color:#ff5630}*please let me know if you’d rather me draft a liability cap that we can negotiate with PPL PRS before proceeding*{color}.



Please let me know once you have had the chance to consider if the business is happy to proceed, with the above in consideration. I’m happy to discuss any of the points and draft clauses to negotiate if needed 🙂 

Many thanks,

Sasha

h3. Summary

* Vertical: Rides; Country: Spain
* The rider has been informed by her driver that her ID is visible to him on the Waybill shared for scheduled rides (See attachment in the ticket).
* Local agent informed CSPC that the drivers indeed receive a document for pre-booked orders which does contain the riders ID. The rider has shown her concern about this. The document can be accessed within our system.

h3. Privacy investigation

When we say 'ID number', do we mean driver's licence number? Or account number? - the rider is concerned by is 02647884d. However, the rider's account ID number is 99710979, so these are not the same.

Based on Spain's Article 24 of Spain’s Orden FOM/36/2008, it looks like a trip sheet is required for each trip, which must in turn contain the ID number of both the operator and the customer. This suggests it is the rider's documentary ID that we are concerned with here - if so, how do we have this in the first place?

*(1) Is this law still in force? (Has it been repealed by Royal Decree 785/2021)?* - No, Article 24 under FOM/36/2008 is no longer in effect _in its original form_, because it was suppressed by [Royal Decree 785/2021|https://cdn.transportes.gob.es/portal-web-sede/documentos/BOE-A-2021-16032-consolidado.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com] once the new electronic service-communications registry came into operation. The transition has already occurred (the registry is active), so one should rely on the new reporting requirement rather than the old trip-sheet model). The old trip sheet with ID of customer & operator obligation no longer applies as a standalone requirement under current law.
*(2) Is the 'customer' here the passenger?* Under the former rule, “customer” meant the party contracting the service (i.e. effectively the passenger or hiring entity). The new reporting regime (785/2021) _does not_ require that user / passenger identity data be reported to the administration.
(3) Even though Bolt must create trip sheets, do these need to be shared with the driver?
(4) Is the ID number at-issue here from the rider's documented ID? If so, when did we collect this from them?

h3. Next steps:

* Confirm questions 3 & 4 with CSPC or stakeholders.
* A response can then be crafted based on whether this is a legal requirement.

* *Your message to me in Slack*: "The driver said he can see the clients ID numbers in the 'Waybill ' What exactly is meant by this, the ongoing order at that time ?"
* *My response:* No, the waybill is this document we generate with the details of the trip and the rider's data. (I will send you the screenshot of the trip attached to the case for more clarity). The name in Spanish is "Hoja de Ruta VTC," and it is a control document that certifies the existence of a pre-booked service for a vehicle with a driver (VTC). It must be in the vehicle, in either physical or digital format, throughout the service. *This document is mandatory for VTCs* and must contain information such as the vehicle's registration number, the names of the driver and rider, as well as the start and end dates and locations of the service, and any other circumstances agreed upon by the parties. The lack of a route sheet is grounds for fines by the transport authorities. *Drivers need the waybill due to Spanish regulations; sometimes the police require this document from them*, and the rider's ID is mentioned there. This is the [link|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/driver-waybill/waybill/150/6109965/1418135205] to the document, but I'm not sure if you have permission, as this is a market-specific document.
* *When did we collect the ID from the rider?* From the moment they attempt to request their first trip in Spain, verification is made, with the subsequent acceptance of the terms and conditions. A photo of the document is required.

On the Torcargo credit line for customs payments:

* *This seems to be standard practice* in the freight/logistics sector. Torcargo’s terms are typical and align with ICC/BIMCO style clauses. Nothing unusual or “red flag” in a legal sense.
* *What it helps with:* gives us up to 15 days to settle customs charges, which can smooth cashflow on imports.
* *What it does* *_not_* *change:* Bolt still carries the underlying liability for customs duties, penalties, and compliance issues. If there are mistakes or late filings, the authorities pursue us, not Torcargo. They also reserve a lien over cargo (i.e. they can hold on to the goods) if payments fall behind.

*Bottom line:* OK to proceed as long as we manage payments on time. It should ease the immediate customs bottleneck, but doesn’t transfer the core risk away from Bolt.

After switching to 75% FTE, the annual entitlement is 26 days of leave at 6 hours each (156 hours in total). There is no reduction to 20 days – what is reduced is the number of hours, not the number of days, if we take your current working day (6 hours) as the unit.

If you are entitled to 26 days on a full-time basis (208h), then after reducing your working time:

* 208h × 0.75 = 156h
* 156h ÷ 6h = *26 days of 6h each*

You’re right that after recalculation your previous 11 full-time days (88h) are now equivalent to *15 days at 6h each*. This is why you see “4 more days” in practice – but it’s not an increase of entitlement, rather a conversion of hours into your new daily schedule.

Hi [~accountid:618124ab3e3753006f742d1c] , sharing the thoughts below:

* The cited law (2025:170) does not clearly impose a legal obligation on private companies such as Bolt to share personal data.
** For context, it seems that the law is applicable to municipalities/public bodies (creating them an obligation to share the data) and it is not clear that this law applies to private companies such as Bolt. Unless Bolt falls under the category of “certain others” (which is not clearly defined), the law does not create a binding obligation to disclose passenger or driver data.
* Under GDPR, disclosure of personal data relating to criminal offences (Article 10 GDPR) requires explicit legal authorisation. That is missing here.
* Therefore, Bolt cannot rely on Article 6(1)(c) GDPR (“legal obligation”) as a basis for disclosure.
* Without a court order or more explicit law, Bolt should not disclose the requested video footage or passenger-related data.



Conclusion: *the legal basis is* +*not valid.*+

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

* *Can u tell me how the Fraud team would decide whether to reactivate a rider?*
The Fraud team doesn’t make this decision. Reactivation is managed by the *Safety team*, based on the blocking matrix. Blocks are applied when a user doesn’t respond to our messages. If the rider replies later and it’s their *first report*, we typically give them another chance.
* *Or would they always reactivate if it was a first report + time has lapsed since the incident (and they missed the comms)?*
If it’s the rider’s *first report* and they *admit to the incident*, their account remains terminated.If they *deny the incident*, we educate and issue a warning.
* *Also, is there not a safety function to send it to (why fraud)?*
Previously, yes. About a year ago, the Safety team managed this process and could unblock riders directly. Since the Fraud team became involved, account blocks now also affect the rider’s device, which requires Fraud’s intervention for reactivation.
*  *why are terminating Riders for an unconfirmed first report?*
According to our SOPs, for *high or significant category cases*, if the rider does not respond within 48 hours, the Cognito tool recommends termination.
* *How do users reach out to us if they have a deactivated account?*
Via Email
* *Lastly, how would the termination decision be different* *_if_* *the rider had responded? Denying an incident wouldn't change the outcome, or would it?*
*First report*: If the rider denies, Cognito recommends a warning.
*Second report*: Termination, with no option for reactivation in the future.
* *Do we email users who do not respond to Bolt notifications or calls?*
Yes. If there’s no response, we send a *termination email*, which often prompts them to reply.
* *Do we always know the agents are always calling?*
No. Calls are *only* made if the *driver* is the accused party. If the *rider* is accused, they are not called.
* *Can we see a few case numbers of the incidents?*
I don’t currently track these cases. The Fraud team may be able to provide specific case references.

Hi [~accountid:712020:6ec9ea6b-f071-41dc-ab0a-54910568f43d] - thanks for the call just now. Summarising what was discussed below.

Based on our discussion, I understand the following to be the case:

* We (Bolt) are not sharing any personal / driver-specific data with Fortum under this arrangement.
* Fortum will be sharing signup and benefit usage data with us. It may be the preference that this is shared on a driver-specific level, rather than aggregated.
* We have not yet shared the partnership agreement with Fortum. It is likely that Fortum will want to include their own data sharing agreement as an annex, regardless of what we include.

As I flagged on the call, the main reason we (Bolt) would push for a DSA here is where *_we are sharing data with a third party_* (rather than the other way around) - this is because we could be ‘on the hook’ if we share personal data with a third party and the third party accidentally leaks / breaches that data. Since this does not apply here, we do not need to be the party pushing for a DSA - it makes more sense for Fortum to be doing this. 

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
As such, the next steps are as follows:

# Remove the Data Sharing Agreement (and its Appendices) completely from the partnership agreement before it is shared with Fortum 
## (This makes sense in any context, as the current draft applies to Africa where Bolt is the exporter, which is not the case here.)
# Determine whether Fortum will be sharing _personal_ or _aggregated_ data with Bolt.
## From a compliance perspective, it would be easier for us if it were aggregated, as it would mean we do not need to enter a DSA / subject ourselves to additional contractual obligations. However, if the business would prefer driver-specific data to be shared, this is something we can do.
# If Fortum will be sharing driver-specific data and they include their own DSA, let me know and I will review it.
{panel}

h3. 🎯 Purpose

When expanding into a *new market or vertical*, all stakeholders must be informed of the *LER process* to ensure alignment, compliance, and consistency in communication with authorities.

h3. Market type

* Determine whether the market is a *Primary* or *Partner* market.
* For *Partner markets*: confirm data sharing agreements and identify who is responsible for LER handling.
* For *Primary markets*: establish stakeholder responsibilities (CS, Ops, Office Manager, Public Policy, GM).

h3. Customer Support (CS)

* Confirm the *responsible CS person* for LER handling in the market.
* If CS is newly introduced, align with *Lisanna Lomp* and confirm Global Guidelines & training on:
** Recognizing valid requests
** Escalation paths
** Data disclosure rules
* Gathering official authority email domains for routing in Beehive

h3. Local Operations (Ops)

* Provide an overview of LERs, personal data, and obligations under data protection laws.
* Clarify when and how Ops may receive requests from authorities.
* Define a clear escalation path (CS → CS Privacy Compliance → Risk Team).
* Communicate what *must NOT be done* (e.g., no direct data sharing, no replies without approval).

h3. Office Manager

* Prepare for postal requests (letters, official mail).
* Ensure Office Managers know the first point of escalation (Local CS or Risk Team).
* Brief on Dawn Raid & Authority Office Visit guidelines (WIP).

h3. Public Policy

* Align with Public Policy on the LER process.
* Share the escalation flowchart for consistent authority communication.
* Keep Public Policy informed of sensitive or high-risk cases due to their authority relationships.

h3. General Managers (GMs)

* Align with the GM on the LER process.
* Share the escalation flowchart so messaging remains consistent across all stakeholders.

{quote}*Context.* In FR we must guarantee *€30 per utilized hour* (pick-up + trip). By policy, *driver incentives must be excluded* from the guarantee calculation so that the top-up only covers *earnings from the work performed* during the guaranteed window.*1) Why current* {{driver_referral}} *is not compliant*

* The single {{driver_referral}} bucket mixes two very different flows:
** *Referrer (the sponsor)* → acquisition bounty, *not tied to their own hours* in the guarantee window. Including it would artificially inflate “earnings per hour” and *reduce/deny top-up* they’re owed.
** *Referee (new driver)* → onboarding/activation bonus typically *conditional on trips/hours*, functioning as a complement to their activity in the period. Excluding it would cause *double top-up* (we’d top up to €30/h on top of the onboarding bonus).
* With one subtype we cannot apply the “exclude referrer / include referee” rule → risk of *underpayment* (referrer) or *overpayment* (referee) versus the €30/h scheme.

# *Why a new subtype is needed*

* We need to distinguish:
** {{driver_referral_referrer}} → *EXCLUDE* from guarantee calc.
** {{driver_referral_referee}} → *INCLUDE* in guarantee calc (prevents double-compensation).
* This clean split lets us compensate them correctly (acquisition expense vs. earnings supplement), and lets Ops/audit trace the guarantee computation unambiguously.

# *Legal/Tax/Controlling confirmation*

* Initial alignment: FR guarantee = *top-up on work-linked income only*; acquisition bounties must not offset the guarantee. This is consistent with our existing “exclude incentives from guarantee” principle.

{quote}

The basis for calculating the Service F is the amount w/o VAT. The quick reconciliation for reference added here: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1dpIJLwe5hO3LavxHQWi6M3IDW4RIHDxCdnSPumcEZpA/edit?usp=sharing|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1dpIJLwe5hO3LavxHQWi6M3IDW4RIHDxCdnSPumcEZpA/edit?usp=sharing|smart-link] 

The SF can be calculated as following:

* The company had Rides for the amount w/o VAT = 120.24, 10% SF = 12.02 pln; SF w VAT = 12.02 * 1.23 = 14.78 pln
* Part of Coupons, is issued to Users of BA and is invoiced with VAT (1st Invoice Row). The amount w/o VAT is 185.19 pln, applying the 10% SF results in the w/o VAT SF of around 18.52. SF w VAT = 18.52 * 1.23 = 22.78 pln
* Other part of Coupons, is issued to not Users of BA. They are out of scope of VAT, so the SF is calculated on the full amount. Taking the 10% SF results in 60.85 pln. SF w VAT = 60.847 * 1.23 = 74.84.

Summing the SF calculations up:

SF w VAT = 12.02 + 18.52 + 60.85 = 112.40, the remaining 14 cents difference is due to the rounding. Please, see on the google sheets, when the values in column E are rounded to two symbols (column F), the amounts become identical.

Hope that makes it clear

+*BACKGROUND*+

* As general background, street-hailing is not generally recommended (unless a tender requirement - see Dubai), due to safety/CS issues.
** If a rider loses an item or wants to complain about a driver, they have no means of identifying the trip / driver to Bolt.
** If the driver wants to raise a complaint against a passenger, Bolt has no means of contacting the later.
** If a rider requests a refund, they can probably only get it by sharing (sensitive) bank details with Bolt.
** Drivers are at a greater risk from a privacy POV, since the rider is not verified.
** Certain safety features (e.g., ratings) are not available for these types of trips.
* Bolt intends to launch the street-hailing feature in Tallinn airport as soon as possible.
** This is a contractual requirement for operating in the taxi lane - we can only do so if we allow street-hailing. As such, even though usually this feature is not recommended, the business wants to implement it in this case.
** On a call with Aleksis and Galina on 2 Oct (the “*Call*”), it was acknowledged that initially Bolt would be implementing cash rides here (and so this would not be commercially profitable for Bolt, due to no commission). However, the business still wants to push ahead as ultimately we are taking market share from ur competitors, and this issue can be addressed in the long term.
** It appears we will be contracting with Forus on this, who has taxis equipped with taximeters. Alternatively, this will be supplied by our own fleet.
*** We are aiming to start working on a contract ASAP - October at the latest.
* Street-hailing effectively works as an ‘offline trip’, since it does not require the rider to have an account - see [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PRODWIKI/pages/5582684630/Street+hailing] and [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1PdNR42qTZ1sjE9Ykd0DsTlf4P8mxM49wBr4P9BlRTPc/edit?tab=t.0]).
** Order flow for drivers is as follows:
*** 1. Driver collects the rider, who has waved them down at the designated street-hailing area.
*** 2. Driver creates the order on the Home Screen (cannot be created during an active ride) by clicking “New ride”. Driver then manually inputs the destination address, based on specifications from the rider.
*** 3. Driver is then shown predicted price (based on current driver location and input destination), and payment option selector (terminal or cash - no in-app payments are available). This shows the price that the rider should pay to the driver (effectively directly).
**** NB. In Estonia, initial plan is to push for cash rides (per discussions on the Call). This makes Bolt commission problematic.
*** 4. Driver then clicks “Start Ride”. On Bolt’s systems, this skips the ‘Driving to Pickup’ and ‘Waiting for Client’ periods, and goes directly to ‘Driving with Client’.
**** Driver is able to add additional stops, as in usual flow. 
*** 5. Once destination reached, final price is shown, without any option to change it (or for either user to rate each other).
**** Once confirmation button pressed, driver is then once again available for usual dispatching.
** Order flow for riders is as follows:
*** 1. Rider waves down the driver at the designated street-hailing area. No app required.
*** 2. Rider verbally tells the driver the destination.
*** 3. Driver shows the rider the final price at the end of the trip.
*** 4. Rider scans a QR code to get an invoice at the end of the trip (provided on the driver’s app - see [here|https://www.figma.com/design/w2niHj1ngpy5Lzy4jK4R4K/Active-Ride?node-id=14420-15541&t=QhuHqZtEf5BIYM2b-0]).
**** Usual Bolt invoice is then shown to them. Recipient listed as “Private Client”. Does not appear that driver details are listed. _However_, this may not be the latest version…
* The business is primarily concerned by the fact that passengers and drivers are unable to report each other in-app - this is the purpose of the parent ticket.
* *Requests*:
** On the Call, I flagged I would do a general privacy assessment of the feature to check for red flags.
** The business has also asked the following:
*** _1. What driver information can be displayed inside the vehicle (e.g. name, driver ID, plate number)?_
*** _2. Should Bolt contact details also be displayed to ensure that in case of a safety incident passengers can reach out and reference the correct driver? If yes, what can we display?_
*** _3. Are there any options or ways for the drivers to report passengers at all?_

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Central EU assessment is here: [{color:#ff5630}+*LINK*+{color}|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ZRzP-BST9cdLgHU-BS5v1XP20BQjMoMX/edit]
** Data processing of the driver is not substantially different here. Main difference is that we are processing less rider data (i.e., trip info and any subsequent complaints data) under a different setup. No DPIA needed at this time.
** NB. Estonia’s Personal Data Protection Act supplements the GDPR - no particular carve-outs relating to this feature. As such, GDPR principles apply.
* Key points are:
** *Legal basis*: Difficult to rely on contractual necessity for processing offline passenger data, since the passenger has not entered into our T&Cs (this mainly impacts ‘enabling the transport services’ and ‘calculating prices’). Instead, we would need to rely on legitimate interest / legal obligation for passenger data (which is ultimately manageable). Also, we cannot rely on the rider’s consent for any safety features (not a concern for ATR as we do not need consent in EE - may not be an issue overall, but I do not have full visibility). :orange_circle: 
** *Transparency:* Offline passengers are not currently covered in our privacy notices (which only cover “_persons arranging passenger rides services via the Bolt App_”), and since passengers do not have the app, they cannot access transparency info easily. This is low risk, as the data we are processing is minimal (only concrete category is complaint/report - although technically trip details / invoice are the rider’s data as well, this is more of a grey area since we have no way of actually linking the trip to a specific rider). As a mitigation measure, we can include a link / disclaimer language in the invoice / complaints flow, until updates are later made to the passenger PN. :green_circle: 
** *User complaints / safety / DSARs*: Currently, there is no real way for the driver and passenger to complain about the other, nor for us to verify a rider’s identity if they submit a DSAR. Possible mitigations would be the generation of a trip token / ID with the ride receipt and asking rider to confirm trip details (for passengers) (or alternatively, if driver info will be displayed anyway, they can use that), and for refund use a time-limited secure form segregated from core ride data; restrict access; delete bank details after processing. 🔴 
** *Integration*: If we engage a third-party fleet (as an independent controller), we should ensure only proportionate integration to Bolt’s systems. It would also be worth having a data sharing agreement in place. :green_circle: 
** *Unintended disclosure*: Anyone with access to the QR code would have access to the trip receipt (although low risk). As such, this should be time-limited. :green_circle: 
* NB. Local Estonian law (non-privacy) is the main constraint - If the trip is treated as a _classic taxi_ (and not an ‘information society service’ being provided to the rider), then the following are required: (i) taximeter; (ii) printed receipt; and (iii) displayed driver service card. Using only app-based services and QR receipts would go against this.
** Engaging a taximeter-equipped fleet may be a means of getting around this (it seems this is what the business is already doing with Forus). t is that or get comfort from the regulator.
** _However_, this should be limited only to what local law requires (i.e., service provider card, vehicle plate, carrier name). No ID cards.

* Questions:
** What precise data will be included on passenger invoices?
** How does the taximeter work in tandem with the price prediction in the Bolt app - is it integrated? If so, what is the extent of the integration?
** Will drivers be able to use all typical safety features enabled in EE during offline trips?
** Presumably this functionality will only be available to drivers located geographically in the airport?
* Provide business with an overview of the core advice.
* Responses to business Qs:
** 1. We should only be providing what is strictly required by local Estonian law (e.g., Public Transport Act) - I defer to Regional Legal on this, but it should be service provider card, vehicle plate and carrier name.
** 2. Yes. This should either be a dedicated email address or a link to an online form, which should be integrated with relevant CS / safety channels to ensure it is escalated properly.
** 3. This is an Ops question (and a difficult one at that). Not a privacy law issue for us to comment on.

I’ve done some thinking on this and here’s what I think. 

From a legal side, I don’t think we should disable Custom Pricing in the UK, even temporarily. Auto-Accept is valuable in its own way (control over workload/conditions) and could become a stronger defence in practice if adoption is high. But for now the safest approach is to keep both live and frame Auto-Accept as complementary.

It seems to us that the customer is mixing up two different things:

* Administrative offense procedures (contraordenações rodoviárias), which are indeed covered by the Código da Estrada (Highway Code) and the Regime Geral das Contraordenações (RGCO), with their own deadlines and notifications handled by the autoridade administrativa (e.g., ANSR, municipality).
* Contractual liability between Bolt and the rider, where Bolt, as operator of the scooter, is billed for municipal fines and can in turn recover the cost from the customer under Bolt’s Terms & Conditions.

The user was not fined directly by the municipality. Bolt received the fine as the registered operator/owner of the scooter, then re-charged it to the user responsible for the trip. In this case, deadlines of the RGCO about notification to the offender don’t apply to Bolt’s internal recharging — Bolt is not acting as an “autoridade administrativa”, but simply passing on the cost it was legally required to pay.

If this is the case, I suggest the following response:

*EN:*
_Dear xxxxxxx,_

_Thank you for your message and for sharing your perspective on this matter._

_We would like to clarify how the process works in cases like yours:_

* _When a scooter is found in breach of local parking or traffic rules, the competent authority (e.g., the Municipality of Lisbon) issues the fine to Bolt as the registered operator of the vehicle. Bolt is therefore legally responsible for paying this fine, regardless of who was using the scooter at the time._
* _In turn, under our Terms and Conditions accepted by all users before riding, Bolt has the right to recharge these costs to the customer who was operating the scooter when the violation occurred. This mechanism does not mean that Bolt is acting as the municipality or as an administrative authority, but simply recovering a cost it was obliged to pay on your behalf._
* _For this reason, the timelines and notification rules under the Regime Geral das Contraordenações do not apply to you directly. Those rules govern the relationship between the issuing authority and Bolt as the fined entity. Bolt, once notified and charged, may recover the corresponding amount from the customer responsible for the trip, even if some time has passed._

_We understand your concern regarding the timing of the notification. In practice, fines are often communicated to Bolt by the municipality several months after the original event, and we can only recharge customers once we receive the official notice. This explains why you were informed later, but it does not affect the validity of the charge._

_To summarise:_

* _The fine was issued by the Municipality to Bolt._
* _Bolt paid it as the responsible vehicle operator._
* _In line with our Terms and Conditions, the cost was recharged to your account._
* _This recharge does not constitute an “administrative sanction” against you, but rather the contractual passing on of a cost incurred due to your use of the vehicle._

_We hope this explanation clarifies the situation. Please be assured that we are committed to transparency, and we only ever recharge amounts that we have been formally required to pay as vehicle operator._

_If you have further questions, we remain at your full disposal._

_Best regards,_

 

*PT:*
_Cara xxxxxxx,_

_Agradecemos a sua mensagem e por partilhar a sua perspetiva sobre esta situação._

_Gostaríamos de esclarecer como funciona o processo em casos como o seu:_

* _Quando uma trotinete é encontrada em violação das regras locais de estacionamento ou trânsito, a autoridade competente (por exemplo, o Município de Lisboa) emite a coima à Bolt, como operadora registada do veículo. Assim, a Bolt é legalmente responsável pelo pagamento dessa coima, independentemente de quem estava a utilizar a trotinete no momento da infração._
* _Por sua vez, nos termos e condições aceites por todos os utilizadores antes de iniciarem uma viagem, a Bolt tem o direito de cobrar estes custos ao cliente que estava a utilizar a trotinete no momento da infração. Este mecanismo não significa que a Bolt esteja a atuar pelo Município ou como uma autoridade administrativa, mas apenas a recuperar um custo que foi obrigada a pagar em seu nome._
* _Por este motivo, neste caso os prazos e regras de notificação previstos no Regime Geral das Contraordenações não lhe são diretamente aplicáveis. Essas regras regulam a relação entre a entidade autuante (o Município) e a Bolt, como entidade autuada. A Bolt, uma vez notificada e cobrada, pode recuperar o valor correspondente junto do cliente responsável pela viagem, mesmo que já tenha passado decorrido algum tempo._

_Compreendemos a sua preocupação relativamente ao momento da notificação. Na prática, as coimas são muitas vezes comunicadas à Bolt pelo Município vários meses após a prática da infração, e só podemos repercutir o valor ao cliente após receção da respetiva notificação. Isto explica porque foi informada mais tarde, mas não afeta a validade da cobrança por parte da Bolt._

_Em resumo:_

* _A coima foi emitida pelo Município à Bolt._
* _A Bolt pagou-a enquanto operadora responsável do veículo._
* _De acordo com os termos e condições aplicáveis, o custo foi repercutido na sua conta._
* _Esta cobrança não constitui uma sanção ou coima administrativa contra si, mas sim a cobrança prevista contratualmente de um custo incorrido pela Bolt devido à sua utilização do veículo._

_Esperamos que esta explicação tenha ajudado a esclarecer a situação. Reiteramos o nosso compromisso com a transparência e garantimos que apenas recuperamos os montantes que fomos formalmente obrigados a pagar enquanto operadora do veículo._

_Caso tenha outras questões, permanecemos inteiramente à disposição._

_Com os melhores cumprimentos,_

If the payment is processed directly to the Driver’s or Fleet Owner’s (FO’s) account via the card terminal, then:

* The Driver/FO is the “merchant” in the payments chain, as they are the party accepting the customer’s card payment.
* The merchant agreement / card terminal contract must therefore be in the Driver’s or FO’s name, not Bolt’s.
* The acquiring bank or PSP will carry out onboarding and due diligence on the Driver/FO as their customer, not on Bolt.
* Bolt’s role is limited to facilitating this payment option in the app (similar to enabling cash), without acting as an acquirer or payment intermediary — which keeps Bolt outside of direct regulatory obligations under the _Financial Institutions Act (Cap. 376) / PSD2 (Second Payment Services Directive)._

*Implications for Bolt*

* Verify that Drivers/FOs using this method are registered with a PSP and have an active terminal contract.
* Request and store confirmation (or Merchant ID) from the Driver/FO.
* Keep this documentation on the Driver/FO profile (since liability rests with the merchant), while terminal details (serial number, assignment) may optionally also be linked to the car profile.
* Our T&Cs already expressly cover in-vehicle card terminal payments, so no contractual updates are needed.

*Documents to collect from each Driver/FO:*

# Merchant Contract (showing FO/Driver name and PSP details).
# Bank Account Details (settlement account in the same name, verified against existing onboarding KYC).
# Terminal Details (serial number / ID, and assignment to vehicle if relevant).

Hey [~accountid:712020:f63df97f-cad1-4718-9bb1-80038488d7e2] ! Not sure if you just need me to validate the answers you already drafted, or if you also want me to provide information for the others that have nothing written by you, so I will do both ☺️ 

*In* [*this doc:*|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1br2v8FkWX55Kg-gZrmJzcweZOFRo3apVYnc9Q1UQ4R4/edit?gid=0#gid=0]

+*Question 1*+ ✅ 

+*Question 2*+

I just add that for general food and drinks, no sector-specific restrictions apply.

These items can be subject to discounts, subject to general consumer law obligations:

* Transparency: discounts must be clear, not misleading (Decree-Law 70/2007, promotional sales regime).
* Duration: promotional period must be specified.
* Price display: discounts must show the previous price and new price (if item-specific).

+*Question 3*+

Yes,  Portugal requires fiscalised invoicing for restaurants, but this is handled via AT-certified invoicing/POS software, not separate fiscal hardware. Restaurants must issue fiscal receipts with QR/ATCUD codes and report sales data (monthly SAF-T submission, moving toward real-time). For DineOut, the fiscalisation responsibility stays with the restaurant, not Bolt.

The restaurant must:

* Issue a certified fiscal invoice/receipt for the meal.
* Apply discounts/cashbacks correctly in that invoice.
* Ensure that the data is stored and reported to AT.
* Bolt’s role (payment + promotions facilitator) does not create an additional fiscalisation obligation for Bolt, but: If Bolt provides a payment option, the integration must ensure restaurants can still issue fiscalised invoices (e.g., waiter enters full bill in POS, then customer pays through Bolt).


+*Question 4*+

To my understanting, a pre-bill is an informal document given to the customer before payment: tt shows the ordered items and total, so the customer can check before settling the bill (often used when customers split the bill).

* Legal status:
** A pre-bill has no fiscal value.
** It cannot replace an invoice/receipt (fatura/recibo).
** Restaurants must still issue a certified fiscal invoice using their AT-approved software/POS at the time of payment.
* Process:
*# Waiter brings pre-bill (_pré-conta_) for customer verification.
*# Customer pays (cash, card, app, etc.).
*# Restaurant issues the fiscal invoice (with ATCUD + QR code) via certified software.

+*Question 5*+
Yes, waiters can edit open orders after printing a pre-bill. There are *no regulatory restrictions* preventing changes to pre-bills, since they have no fiscal value. Restrictions only apply once the fiscal invoice is issued.

+*Question 6*+
I don’t think it is needed a special authorisation to change an order after printing a pre-bill. Some systems may require a code as an internal control, but this is a technical/business rule, not a legal one.

+*Question 7*+
Yes. Under Decreto-Lei n.º 198/2012 and Portaria n.º 363/2010, all businesses, including restaurants, must issue an invoice for every transaction, regardless of whether the customer asks for it. The invoice must be generated through AT-certified invoicing software/POS.

+*Question 8*+
No.

+*Question 9*+
In practice, many restaurants do ask customers to pay based on the pre-bill (especially when splitting bills). This is not illegal per se, but the restaurant must still issue the fiscal invoice immediately after payment. The actual legal obligation is that the invoice must be generated at the moment of payment — so if the restaurant only provides a pre-bill and does not follow up with a fiscal invoice, that is a tax violation.

+*Question 10*+
To my understanding, for delivery orders it is common that restaurants don’t apply Bolt discounts in their POS, since Bolt manages it in settlement. But in DineOut, because the customer pays the restaurant directly, the discount must be applied in the POS so the fiscal invoice reflects the true final amount.

+*Question 11*+  ✅

Hi [~accountid:712020:80adc2a7-05ca-4e9d-b299-6ace53125c4f] / [~accountid:5ed4b18fc3b5390c24a6f905] - I have taken a look at this from a privacy POV and include my thoughts below. In summary:

* I have provided responses to your questions in *Section 1*.
* I have flagged some core privacy risks regarding street-hailing in Estonia generally in *Section 2*.
* I have summarised some key outstanding questions at *Section 3*.

Happy to discuss this if any of it is unclear 🙂 

----

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(1) Responses to your questions*
{panel}

{quote}# _What driver information can be displayed inside the vehicle (e.g. name, driver ID, plate number)?_{quote}

* My understanding is that the purpose of displaying driver information in the vehicle is so that the passenger can specify the driver to Bolt if they issue a complaint / safety report (please confirm if this is not the case). On this basis, IMO there are better / more privacy-compliant means of enabling this (see further details below in the ‘Privacy Review’ section) - as such, we should not be displaying driver information in the vehicle unless we have a good reason to do so.
* From a quick bit of internet research, local Estonian transport law may require certain driver information to be displayed in the car if the car is considered as a ‘classic taxi’ (per [~accountid:63da287e790148a18093a774]'s previous advice). If this is the case, my understanding is that the inside of the car would in any event need to display: (i) the carrier name; (ii) the vehicle licence plate; and (iii) a ‘service provider card’ containing driver details (although *I defer to Elina to confirm this*).
* If such transport laws do not apply, then I will need to consider this question based on the setup that we agree on (e.g., Forus / Bolt fleet / etc.), as our relationship with the drivers will determine to what extent we can determine what they should be displaying in their vehicles (?) 
* (i)  {color:#4c9aff}+*In short*+{color}: The inside of the car should ideally only display the driver information that is required by local transport law. If such transport laws do not apply, I would be happy to reconsider this question once we have confirmed the setup / relationship with the drivers.

{quote}# _Should Bolt contact details also be displayed to ensure that in case of a safety incident passengers can reach out and reference the correct driver? If yes, what can we display?_{quote}

* In an ideal world, {color:#36b37e}*yes*{color} ✅ This would certainly be beneficial not only from a privacy POV but from a UX POV more generally. {color:#ff5630}*However*{color}, as above, it would firstly be helpful to confirm the setup / relationship with the drivers that is agreed up for this feature, as this will ultimately determine to what extent we can determine what they should be displaying in their vehicles (?) 
* (i) If we do end up telling drivers to include Bolt contact details in their vehicles, this should be either a dedicated email address, phone number or link to a form. It does not matter from my POV what email / phone / link is displayed, provided that this would direct the passenger to the correct team to help address their concerns. This is *more of a question for Ops and Safety*. 

{quote}# _Are there any options or ways for the drivers to report passengers at all?_{quote}

* This is a key concern with the feature from a safety POV - if we are not collecting any account or contact information on the passenger, then practically speaking, {color:#ff5630}+*no*+{color} - it seems that if the driver wanted to report the passenger to Bolt, they would have no way of identifying them (and we would have no way of taking action against the passenger) ❌ 
* If there are any practical solutions that the business can think of, then I would be happy to assess the associated privacy law risks - however, suggesting the options themselves seems to be *more of a question for* *Ops and Safety*. 

----

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(2) Key privacy risks / mitigations*
{panel}

In short, if this feature is a core business priority, then the Privacy Team {color:#36b37e}*will not block it*{color} ✅ 

However, in addition to the obvious safety / UX concerns, there are some key privacy risks that should be addressed. These are summarised below.

||*Issue*||*Priority*||*Advice / Mitigations*||
|*Passenger Complaints / Requests*
As noted in the ticket description, a key issue here is that it is very difficult for users to submit complaints / reports about one another here where the passenger does not have an account and does not provide their contact information. 
This poses the following privacy issues regarding offline passengers who want to submit complaints / queries to Bolt:
* *Data requests*: We are technically processing limited data about offline passengers here (e.g., trip data, invoice information), which we are required to provide the passenger with on request. However, if an offline passenger emails Bolt asking for this information, we currently have no way of linking it to the relevant trip and finding the data. This could lead to the passenger complaining to the data protection authority.
* *Refund requests*: If the passenger requested a refund and (for whatever reason) Bolt decided to provide it, the only way to process this would involve asking the passenger for (sensitive) banking information, which poses privacy risks.|🔴|For *drivers* who want to submit complaints about offline passengers, there is no easy solution to this problem. If we will not be collecting the passenger’s account / contact information, the business may need to accept the risk that it will be difficult to give drivers effective redress here ⚠️ 
For offline *passengers* who want to submit complaints about drivers / data requests, I would recommend the following:
* *Trip token / booking reference number*: Instead of providing driver details in the vehicle (unless this is required- see Section 1 above), it would be sensible to provide the passenger with a booking reference number via the QR code (in addition to their invoice). The passenger could then provide this booking reference number if they submit a complaint, which could allow us to identify the trip on our side. I believe this is being considered as a solution for ‘Bolt Kiosk’ where the issue is effectively the same, and so it makes sense to ensure consistency. 💡 
* *Refunds*: Instead of asking for their bank details over email, the passenger should be provided with a secure form to collect and use their bank details, which ensures that such bank details are subsequently deleted from our systems. 💡|
|*Safety Features*
My understanding is that drivers will still be able to use a lot of core safety features enabled in EE even when using the street-haling feature - is that correct?
If so, then to the extent that any of these features rely on *passenger consent* as a legal basis for processing user data (e.g., Audio Trip Recording, which thankfully is not an issue in EE), then we should not be using them during street-hailing trips since we will have no legal basis to do so (i.e., the passenger cannot consent via the app if they do not have an account). 
Please note that although currently I have not seen any features which obviously pose this risk, I do not have visibility on the setup of every safety feature currently live in Estonia. As such, I cannot comment for certain whether it currently applies.|:orange_circle:|If we identify any safety features live in Estonia which rely on passenger consent to collect and process data, then we will need to find a way to disable them for street-hailing trips ⚠️ 
If this will not be operationally feasible, then it is open to the business to accept the risk of collecting and processing passenger data in a non-compliant manner. However, this could result in privacy complaints and regulatory enforcement.|
|*Third-Party Engagement*
Depending on the setup that we settle on, if we are sharing user data with a third party and integrating their systems with Bolt systems (e.g., if we are somehow linking taximeters to Bolt’s own price calculation systems), we should ensure that this data sharing is properly protected through a contract (i.e., a data sharing agreement).
Otherwise, Bolt may be ‘on the hook’ if we share user data with the third party and that third party uses the data unlawfully / suffers a data breach.|:orange_circle:|Depending on the agreed setup, as part of reviewing the contract with any third party, the Privacy Team should be kept in the loop so that we can draft appropriate data sharing provisions. 💡|
|*Transparency*
Our privacy notices do not currently cover offline passengers, and because we never directly interact with them we do not show them any transparency information that is required under the GDPR. This raises compliance risks if any offline passengers decide to complain about this.|:orange_circle:|We should ideally include some disclaimer language via the QR code that is provided to offline passengers. I can prepare such language if needed. 💡|
|*Unintended* *Disclosure*
Technically, anyone with access to one of the QR codes could access its contents. This creates a risk of unintentionally disclosing offline passenger data to other people, which would count as a personal data breach.|:green_circle:|The QR code should ideally be time-limited (i.e., it should not work indefinitely), which would substantially lower the risk profile. 💡|

----

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(3) Outstanding questions from me*
{panel}

Based on my review, I have the following outstanding questions - {color:#4c9aff}*please review these ASAP*{color}, and I will let you know if this affects any of the above advice:

# What precise information will be included on the passenger invoices? Will any details about the driver be included?
# How will the taximeters work in practice in terms of affecting the predicted and final price presented in the driver’s Bolt app? Will such taximeters be integrated with our systems, and if so to what extent?
# Other than ratings, are there any other safety features that drivers will not be able to use when taking a street-hailing trip?
# Presumably this feature will only be available for drivers who are geographically located in Tallinn airport, right?
# Let me know once we have decided on the final setup (i.e. if we will be using Forus, a Bolt fleet, or another arrangement).
